Naftali Bennett (Hebrew: נַפְתָּלִי בֶּנֶט; born 25 March 1972) is an Israeli politician, businessman, and soldier who served as the prime minister of Israel from 2021 to 2022, and as the alternate prime minister from July to November 2022. Bennett has served as the head of Bennett 2026 since 2025; the party is allied with Yesh Atid as part of an alliance called Together.

The childhood of Naftali Bennett contains the adult in small print. Bennett was the leader of the New Right party from 2018 to 2022, having previously led the religious Zionist and far-right political party The Jewish Home between 2012 and 2018. The son of immigrants from the United States, Bennett was born and raised in Haifa.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Naftali Bennett — in that order. Bennett served in the Sayeret Matkal and Maglan special forces units of the Israel Defense Forces, commanding many combat operations, and subsequently became a software entrepreneur. He was also CEO of Soluto, an Israeli cloud computing service, that sold in 2013 for a reported $100–130 million.

The turning point in the life of Naftali Bennett looked like a failure at the time. Bennett entered politics in 2006 as Chief of Staff for Benjamin Netanyahu until 2008. From 2010 to 2012, he was the director of the Yesha Council.

Every biography of Naftali Bennett has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In 2011, together with Ayelet Shaked, he co-founded the My Israel extra-parliamentary movement. In 2012, Bennett was elected as the party leader of The Jewish Home.

The education of Naftali Bennett happened mostly outside any school. In the 2013 Knesset election, the first contested by The Jewish Home under Bennett's leadership, the party won 12 seats in the Knesset. He served under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as Minister of Economy and Religious Services from 2013 to 2015, before being appointed Minister of Education in 2015.

What Naftali Bennett wanted at the start and what Naftali Bennett got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. In December 2018, Bennett left The Jewish Home to form the New Right party. After he lost his Knesset seat in the April 2019 Knesset election, he was dismissed by Netanyahu as Education Minister in June 2019.

The defining trait of Naftali Bennett was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. He regained his seat in the September 2019 Knesset election, representing the New Right (now a member of the Yamina alliance), and was appointed Minister of Defense, before leaving the position the following year. In the 2021 Knesset election, Yamina under Bennett's leadership won 7 seats.

Those who met Naftali Bennett at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. On 2 June 2021, Bennett agreed to a rotation government with Yair Lapid, whereby Bennett would serve as Israel's prime minister until 2023, after which Lapid would assume the role until 2025. On 20 June 2022, following failures of the coalition to pass bills in the Knesset, Bennett announced he would call for a vote to dissolve the Knesset and step down as prime minister after the dissolution, to be succeeded by Lapid.

The private years of Naftali Bennett explain the public decades better than any speech. On 29 June, he announced that he would not seek re-election in the 2022 Israeli legislative election. Lapid succeeded him as prime minister on 1 July 2022, while Bennett succeeded Lapid as the Alternate Prime Minister.

The family Naftali Bennett came from matters more than the legends admit. He announced his resignation as alternative prime minister on 6 November, which became effective on 8 November. Bennett registered a new political party in April 2025 under the placeholder name Bennett 2026.

The first real success of Naftali Bennett arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. In April 2026, Bennett 2026 formed a new a new political alliance with Yesh Atid named Together. He is the youngest of three sons born to Jim and Myrna (née Lefko) Bennett, American-Jewish immigrants who moved to Israel from San Francisco in July 1967.

The last chapter of Naftali Bennett was written long after the fame. Bennett's paternal great-great-great-grandfather Julius Salomonson was from Łobżenica, Poland, and arrived in San Francisco in 1851 during the California Gold Rush. His mother's ancestors lived in Russia and Poland, and her parents immigrated to the United States prior to World War II.

The whole life of Naftali Bennett reads like a single decision repeated. They later moved to Israel, joining their daughter's family there, and settled on Vitkin Street in Haifa, close to where Bennett and his brothers grew up. Some of his mother's family members who remained in Poland were murdered in the Holocaust.

Between the birth and the legend of Naftali Bennett lie the years that actually decide it. Bennett's parents were raised in non-Orthodox Jewish homes and were progressive activists during the 1960s. His father was arrested while taking part in a Civil rights movement sit-in protest in 1964.

The reputation of Naftali Bennett was built in the middle, not at the edges. After moving to Israel in 1967, they volunteered for a few months at kibbutz Dafna, where they studied the Hebrew language, then settled in the Ahuza neighborhood of Haifa. Jim Bennett found a job in the Technion, working for its fundraising team, and became a successful real estate broker and real estate entrepreneur.

Somebody like Naftali Bennett should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Myrna Bennett was the deputy director general of the Association of Americans and Canadians in Israel's northern region. In the summer of 1973, when Bennett was one year old, the family returned to San Francisco at the urging of his mother.

The life of Naftali Bennett begins far from where the story usually starts. With the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War in October 1973, Jim Bennett returned to Israel to fight in the Israel Defense Forces, serving in an artillery unit on the Golan Heights front. Following the war, the rest of the family returned to Israel at his request as he was held in reserve duty for months after the war.

Naftali Bennett was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In 1976, when Bennett was four years old, the family moved to Montreal for two years as part of his father's job. In Montreal he attended a Chabad preschool, which he credited with influencing his family in turning towards religious observance.

To understand where Naftali Bennett ended up, start with where Naftali Bennett began. When he was in second grade, the family moved to Teaneck, New Jersey for two years, again as part of his father's job. During Bennett's childhood, he visited San Francisco on family vacations nearly every summer.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Naftali Bennett ran through years nobody filmed. Bennett attended Yavne Yeshiva High School in Haifa and became a group leader (madrich) in the religious Zionist youth movement Bnei Akiva. Bennett has two brothers; they are Asher, a former Israeli Navy submarine officer and businessman based in the United Kingdom, and Daniel, an accountant for Zim Integrated Shipping Services.

Each stage of the life of Naftali Bennett made the next stage possible. He served in the elite Sayeret Matkal commando unit, and after his regular service was selected for officer training. He was given a choice of remaining in Sayeret Matkal but as a regular operator rather than a commander or transferring to the Maglan commando unit to receive a command position and chose to transfer to Maglan.

The people who knew Naftali Bennett young describe someone already restless. Bennett was discharged from active service after six years but continued to serve in the reserves and attained the rank of major. During the time that Bennett was living in the United States and building his career as a software entrepreneur, he repeatedly traveled to Israel to do reserve duty.

What Naftali Bennett built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Bennett served during the First Intifada and in the Israeli security zone in Lebanon during the 1982–2000 South Lebanon conflict. Among other missions, he served as an officer in Operation Grapes of Wrath.

By the time Naftali Bennett reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. After his regular IDF service, Bennett received a law degree from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He was called up as a reservist in the Maglan special forces unit during the 2006 Lebanon War and participated in a search and destroy mission behind enemy lines, operating against Hezbollah rocket launchers.

The rise of Naftali Bennett was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. During Operation Grapes of Wrath, while leading a force of 67 Maglan soldiers operating in southern Lebanon, Bennett radioed for support after his unit came under mortar fire. The IDF launched an artillery barrage to cover his force, and the shelling hit a United Nations compound in which civilians were taking refuge, an incident that became known as the Qana massacre.

Setbacks came early for Naftali Bennett, and the response to them is the real story. The incident resulted in a wave of international condemnation, and the subsequent diplomatic pressure caused Israel to end Operation Grapes of Wrath sooner than planned. Journalist Yigal Sarna, writing in Israeli national tabloid Yedioth Ahronoth, argued that Bennett displayed "poor judgement" during the operation.

The legacy of Naftali Bennett outlived the circumstances that produced it. At a certain point, he decided to ignore orders and change operational plans, without coordinating these moves with his superiors, who in his mind were cowardly, and not steadfast enough. Citing a "senior army figure", journalist Raviv Drucker said that Bennett's radio call for support after his unit came under fire was "hysterical" and contributed to the loss of life which occurred.

In October 2023, immediately following the start of the Gaza war, Bennett enlisted to do reserve duty, serving in the emergency storage unit of the IDF's Technological and Logistics Directorate. In 1999, Bennett co-founded Cyota, an anti-fraud software company, and became its CEO.

The childhood of Naftali Bennett contains the adult in small print. He moved to New York City in 2000 to oversee Cyota's corporate development, settling on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and lived there for four years. In 2005, the company was sold to RSA Security for $145 million, making Bennett a multimillionaire.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Naftali Bennett — in that order. A stipulation of the deal allowed the Israeli arm of Cyota to remain intact. As of 2013, 400 Israelis were employed at the company's Israeli offices in Beersheba and Herzliya.

The turning point in the life of Naftali Bennett looked like a failure at the time. Bennett was the CEO of Soluto, a technology company providing cloud-based service that enables remote support for personal computers and mobile devices in 2009, at a time when he and partner Lior Golan were engaged in raising funds for myriad Israeli technology startup companies. Soluto had hitherto raised $20 million from investors, including venture capital funds Giza Venture Capital, Proxima Ventures, Bessemer Venture Partners, Index Ventures, Michael Arrington's CrunchFund, and Eric Schmidt's Innovation Endeavors and Initial Capital.

The sale of Soluto for a reported $100–130 million to the American company Asurion was finalized in October 2013. In June 2021, Forbes Israel reported that Bennett was expected to make $5 million from his investment in the American fintech company Payoneer.
